questions.prompt: User text is inserted into an HTML attribute. Which defense matches the context?

choices.text: Use SQL parameterization on the string before rendering.
Decode HTML entities before inserting untrusted text.
Apply one JavaScript escaping rule to every output context.
Encode for a quoted HTML attribute.

questions.explanation: Encoding must match the browser parsing context. SQL controls do not secure HTML, and decoding can restore dangerous syntax.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Output encoding depends on HTML, attribute, JavaScript or URL context; generic encoding does not make dangerous contexts safe.

questions.prompt: A comment should appear as plain text. Which DOM assignment avoids interpreting its markup?

choices.text: Construct a script element from the comment text.
Remove spaces and then pass it to document.write.
Assign it through textContent.
Assign it through innerHTML without sanitization.

questions.explanation: textContent treats the value as text. HTML-parsing and code-executing sinks can interpret attacker-controlled content.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Untrusted HTML requires sanitization; textContent is a safe text sink while innerHTML parses markup.

questions.prompt: Why can a forged cross-site request act as a logged-in user when sessions use cookies?

choices.text: The request automatically proves the user intended the action.
The browser can attach eligible cookies automatically.
The attacker must read the cookie value before causing an authenticated request.
HttpOnly cookies cannot accompany requests triggered by another site.

questions.explanation: Cookie attachment can supply authentication without proving intent. TLS does not prevent induced authenticated requests.

sources.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Browsers attach eligible cookies automatically; state-changing requests need validated CSRF defenses.

questions.prompt: An app enables SameSite cookies and removes all other CSRF defenses. What is the problem?

choices.text: SameSite is a layer, not a universal replacement.
SameSite always disables all same-origin requests.
SameSite turns every cookie into a bearer header.
SameSite prevents injected scripts from running at all.

questions.explanation: OWASP treats SameSite as defense in depth. It does not stop XSS or replace all application-specific request validation.

sources.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SameSite is defense in depth and XSS can bypass CSRF controls; state-changing GET requests should be avoided.

questions.prompt: A developer encodes a string for HTML and then places it inside executable JavaScript. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: HTML encoding automatically covers every browser parser.
A signed-in user cannot submit an XSS payload.
TLS changes script parsing into safe plain-text rendering.
The encoding may not protect the JavaScript context.

questions.explanation: HTML and JavaScript have different parsing rules. Authentication and transport security do not change the output context.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Encoding must match the destination parsing context.

questions.prompt: A rich-text feature intentionally allows user-supplied HTML. Which control fits that requirement?

choices.text: Delete quote characters but preserve all elements and handlers.
Rely on SQL escaping to remove browser executable content.
Use a maintained HTML sanitizer.
Render every string unchanged because markup is intended.

questions.explanation: A sanitizer evaluates allowed HTML constructs. Intended markup still contains attack surfaces, and ad hoc string edits or SQL escaping are insufficient.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Sanitization is needed when users are permitted to submit HTML markup.

questions.prompt: Which encoding statements help prevent XSS? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use output encoding appropriate to the destination context.
Quote attribute values when inserting encoded text.
Assume HTML encoding makes every script-body insertion safe.
Decode untrusted entities immediately before rendering them.
Encoding once before storage secures every later browser output context.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Different parsers need different escaping rules. B is correct: Quoted attributes reduce parsing ambiguity. C is incorrect: JavaScript contexts need their own controls and dangerous contexts should be avoided. D is incorrect: Decoding may reintroduce executable syntax. E is incorrect: Encoding must fit each destination context rather than one generic storage transformation.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Output encoding depends on HTML, attribute, JavaScript or URL context; generic encoding does not make dangerous contexts safe.

questions.prompt: Which practices distinguish plain text from allowed HTML? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Sanitize untrusted HTML when markup must be supported.
Modify sanitized HTML arbitrarily and assume it remains safe.
Keep the sanitizer updated as bypasses are discovered.
Use innerHTML as a universally safe sink for untrusted strings.
Use textContent for content intended to remain plain text.

questions.explanation: A is correct: A sanitizer removes unsafe constructs. B is incorrect: Later mutations can invalidate sanitization. C is correct: Sanitizer maintenance addresses known weaknesses. D is incorrect: innerHTML interprets HTML and can introduce XSS. E is correct: It avoids parsing the string as HTML.

sources.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Untrusted HTML requires sanitization; textContent is a safe text sink while innerHTML parses markup.

questions.prompt: Which CSRF-token practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Put a secret synchronizer token in URLs for easier logging.
Treat possession of the session cookie as proof of user intent.
A CSRF token is valid whenever its format matches, without server-side verification.
Validate the token on protected state-changing requests.
Keep synchronizer tokens secret and unpredictable.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: URLs can expose tokens through logs and navigation. B is incorrect: Cookie attachment is automatic. C is incorrect: The server must validate the token rather than check only its syntax. D is correct: The server must enforce the token check. E is correct: Attackers should not be able to forge valid tokens.

sources.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Browsers attach eligible cookies automatically; state-changing requests need validated CSRF defenses.

questions.prompt: Which choices support CSRF defense in depth? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use origin checks where appropriate as an additional signal.
Accept any cross-site write merely because the session is valid.
Use SameSite cookies alongside appropriate request validation.
Avoid state-changing operations behind GET routes.
Assume CSRF tokens neutralize every injected script.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Origin validation can supplement token protections. B is incorrect: Authentication alone does not establish request intent. C is correct: Independent controls reduce reliance on one browser behavior. D is correct: Safe navigation should not mutate protected state. E is incorrect: XSS can bypass CSRF defenses.

sources.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SameSite is defense in depth and XSS can bypass CSRF controls; state-changing GET requests should be avoided.
